blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: T he first half National Government Budget Implementation Review Report covers 1 st July to 31 st  December 2025 and is the second report for FY 2025/26. The report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports to Parliament for the National and County governments.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The FY 2025/26 is the third budget under the fourth Medium-Term Plan (MTP) (2023-2027) of the Kenya Vision 2030 and is being implemented under the Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) framework. Under this framework, the government aims to achieve economic turnaround and inclusive growth by increasing investments in at least five sectors that significantly impact the economy and household welfare. These sectors include Agricultural Transformation, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Housing and Settlement, Healthcare, Digital Superhighway, and Creative Industry. The agenda also focuses on increasing employment, equitable income distribution, and social security, while expanding the tax base and boosting foreign exchange earnings.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The National Government's original gross budget for FY 2025/26 was Kshs.4.69 trillion, compared to Kshs.4.37 trillion for FY 2024/25. This comprises Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which was 16 per cent of the original gross national budget and 29 per cent of the original gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised the ministerial recurrent allocation of Kshs.1.80 trillion (38 per cent of the original gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.14 trillion (46 per cent of the original gross national budget). Notably, the Education Sector received the highest budget allocation of Kshs.703.07 billion, followed by Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communication Technology Kshs.534.63 billion, reflecting their key role in the economy.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted funds from various revenue sources, including Tax and Non-Tax Revenue, Borrowing (both external and domestic), grants, other domestic  financing,  and  ministerial  Appropriations-in-Aid (A-IA). During the reporting period, receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.2.17 trillion, representing 49 per cent of the original net estimates of Kshs.4.43 trillion, compared to the Kshs.1.74 trillion (41 per cent) received in the same period in FY 2024/25. The total exchequer issues from the Consolidated Fund to Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Consolidated Fund Services, and the County Governments amounted to Kshs. 2.14 trillion, representing 48 per cent of the original net estimates of Kshs.4.43 trillion, compared to Kshs.1.71 trillion recorded in a similar period in FY 2024/25. The exchequer issues comprised Kshs. 145.05 billion, representing 36 per cent of the annual net estimates for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.809.19 billion, representing 55 per cent of the net yearly estimates for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs. 1.02 trillion, representing 48 per cent of Consolidated Fund Services and Kshs.172.23 billion, representing 42 per cent of the annual net estimates to County governments as Equitable shareable revenue. The Consolidated Fund Services comprise public debt (Kshs.941.61 billion), Pensions and Gratuities (Kshs.73.80 billion), Salaries, Allowances to Constitutional Office Holders, and Miscellaneous Services (Kshs.1.79 billion).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The National Government's total expenditure for the first half of FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.2.18 trillion, representing 47 per cent of the National Government's original gross estimates of Kshs.4.69 trillion compared
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: to Kshs.1.76 trillion (40 per cent) recorded in a similar FY 2024/25 period. This expenditure comprises ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.276.92 billion (with an absorption rate of 37 per cent), recurrent ministerial expenditure at Kshs.899.74 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent) and CFS expenditure at Kshs.1.01 trillion (an absorption rate of 47 per cent).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Development expenditure with the highest spending included Capital Transfers to the MDAs in subsidies, grants and direct transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) at Kshs.169.55 billion, representing 62 per cent of the gross development spending. Other major development expenditures were the Construction and Civil Works at Kshs.62.75 billion and the Purchase of Specialised Plant, Equipment and Machinery at Kshs.9.13 billion, representing 23 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively, of the gross development expenditure. The State Department for Housing and Urban Development recorded the highest ministerial expenditure (in absolute terms) of Kshs.58.89 billion under the construction and civil works category.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.337.63 billion was spent on Compensation to Employees, representing 38 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs and 25 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally, which is in line with the Regulation 26(1) (a) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations 2015 which set a limit that compensation to employees shall not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally and other revenues generated by the national government pursuant to Article 209(4) of the Constitution. Total Current transfers to other government institutions were Kshs.348.79 billion and subsidies of Kshs.56.70 billion, representing 40 per cent and 7 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure, respectively. Other items with significant expenditures included Insurance costs at Kshs.21.44 billion, Security operations at Kshs.22.20 billion, comprising Kshs.9.85 billion by the State Department for Internal Security, Kshs.7.56 billion by the National Treasury and Kshs.4.79 billion by the National Police Service, and travel costs at Kshs.10.87 billion. Travel cost comprises Kshs.7.74 billion and Kshs.3.13 billion for domestic and foreign expenditure, respectively, which is against the 2025 Budget Policy Statement theme on expenditure reforms to cut non-essential expenses. The Teacher Service Commission recorded the highest expenditure (in absolute terms) at Kshs.196.55 billion, attributed to the Teacher Management Programme.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: As of 31 December 2025, the Public debt stock stood at Kshs.12.29 trillion, comprising Kshs.5.46 trillion owed to external lenders (44 per cent) and Kshs.6.82 trillion due to domestic lenders (56 per cent). The public debt stock increased by 4 per cent from Kshs.11.80 trillion as of 30 June 2025, equivalent to 67.8 per cent of the GDP , 1 exceeding the 55 per cent threshold as approved by Parliament to Kshs.12.29 trillion as of 31 December 2025. External debt declined by 0.5 per cent due to repayments, while domestic debt recorded an 8 per cent growth attributable to increased borrowing through Treasury bills and bonds in the domestic market.  Total expenditure on public debt in the first six months of FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.923.14 billion, representing 49 per cent of the approved estimates, comprising external debt servicing Kshs.377.24 billion and domestic debt payment of Kshs 545.90 billion, respectively.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that should be addressed to ensure seamless budget implementation not only in the current financial year but also for posterity. These included low absorption of the development budget, incomplete automation of the procurement and exchequer processes for National Government entities, and an upsurge in the use of Supplementary Budget under Article 223 of the Constitution for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: The upsurge in the use of Article 223 of the Constitution in the first six months was mainly towards other operating expenses and the buyback of an International Sovereign Bond. The Controller of Budget approved Kshs.115.11 billion, comprising Kshs.8.66 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.106.44 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 2 per cent of the gross estimates. Of the total exchequer issues under Article 223 of the Constitution, issuance of an International sovereign bond for liability management operations in the FY2025/2026 received Kshs.86.29 billion, representing 75 per cent of the total requests.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends collaboration of all Stakeholders in the implementation of the Electronic Government Procurement System, including its integration with IFMIS, training of users, both staff and suppliers and technical support to fast-track procurement of the planned activities. Also, the National Treasury should automate the exchequer process for all the votes to foster efficiency and effectiveness in budget implementation.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Further, the Controller of Budget recommends adopting sound planning, budget practices, and effective expenditure management by prioritising essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation. This will reduce the use of Article 223 of the Constitution on budget items that were foreseeable during the budget process and could not be accommodated during the sector working groups due to resource constraints. Good budget implementation practices will enhance fiscal responsiveness, ensuring accountability and budget credibility.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: 1.  INTRODUCTION
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: T he Controller of Budget prepared this report in fulfilment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: This report is in line with Section 9(2) of the Controller of Budget Act Cap 429, which outlines the information to be reported by the Controller of Budget in the quarterly budget implementation reports. In addition, it is aligned with Section 9(5) of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which states that, despite the first quarterly report submitted under Section 9, each subsequent report shall contain cumulative amounts from the beginning of that year. To meet the legal requirements governing the content of budget implementation review reports, the report is presented in seven chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter two presents the performance of receipts into the Consolidated Fund and Exchequer Issues to Ministries, Departments and Agencies, Consolidated Fund Services and the County Revenue Fund as part of the equitable share of revenue to the forty-seven counties. Exchequer issues performance is expressed as a percentage of the annual net estimates.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Three presents the overall budget performance of the national government, including performance under the Consolidated Fund Services, Ministerial expenditure by economic classification, and the stock of Trade Payables (pending bills) for national government entities.   Chapter Four presents the budget performance of the eighty-seven MDAs clustered into ten Sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, which is planned to support fiscal analysis by breaking down government fiscal statistics for comparability. It presents the approved budget referred to as the gross estimates, accrued expenditure, which is further disaggregated into programme and sub-programmes performance and project implementation for MDAs. The absorption rate, which measures the performance, is calculated as a proportion of expenditure relative to the annual budget.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: The number of MDAs increased from eighty-one in FY 2024/25 to eighty-seven in FY 2025/26. Additional MDAs were created through Executive Order No. 1 of 2025, which repealed Executive Order No. 2 of 2023 and dissolved the State Department for Performance and Delivery Management, and established an additional seven State Departments. They include the State Department for National Government Coordination, Science Research and Innovation, Public Investments and Assets Management, Special Programmes, Aviation and Aerospace Development, Children Services and Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs. Their mandates are expounded in their respective sectors in Chapter 4 of the report.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Five presents the key issues identified by the Controller of Budget as hindering effective budget implementation and provides recommendations to address them. Chapter six presents emerging issues that the government should deal with to address fiscal constraints. Chapter Seven provides the conclusion.

blocks.text: 2.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter presents the receipts into the Consolidated Fund and funds released by the National Treasury in the first six months of FY 2025/2026. The funds released went towards funding Consolidated Fund Services, ministerial development expenditure, recurrent expenditure, and transfers to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: The Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose, or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all fees collected by national government entities for services be deposited into the e-citizen account under Paybill number 222222.
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted various revenue sources to raise funds. The sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.63 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.127.65 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.10 trillion - comprising net domestic borrowing of Kshs.634.75 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.463.51 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.561.81 billion), and other domestic financing (Kshs.10.80 billion). The Government also targeted to raise Kshs.672 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.334.26 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.337.74 billion development A-I-A.

blocks.text: 2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution
heading_path: 2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Article 223 of the Constitution allows the national government to access additional funding during the budget implementation by spending money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need for unbudgeted expenditure arises for which no amount has been appropriated, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund.
heading_path: 2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: The total approved additional funding by the Cabinet Secretary, National Treasury, amounted to Kshs.177.46 billion, comprising Kshs.45.06 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.132.42 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 4 per cent of the gross national budget. This was within the Constitutional threshold of ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament in any particular financial year (Kshs.4.69 trillion for FY 2025/26) in line with Article 223(5) of the Constitution.
heading_path: 2.4.5  Exchequer Issues Under Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2025/2026, exchequer issues pursuant to Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya was Kshs.115.11 billion, comprising Kshs.8.66 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.106.45 billion for recurrent expenditure, representing 2 per cent of the annual gross estimates, compared to 0.04 per cent (Kshs.16.95 billion), issued in a similar period of FY2024/2025.

blocks.text: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund
heading_path: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: The Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund to provide only essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.
heading_path: 2.4.6  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget authorised 12 requests amounting to Kshs.1.11 billion from the Equalization Fund. The amount comprised Kshs.68.16 million for Policy 1 development pending bills in favour of the Ministry of Water and Sanitation and Kshs.955.37 million for the Second Policy development projects in 13 County Governments.

blocks.text: 3.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter presents an overview of the National Government budget implementation in the first six months of FY 2025/26. It also presents the budget performance of the Consolidated Fund Services (classified as recurrent expenditure), which contains information on Public debt, Pensions and gratuities, Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional officeholders, and Miscellaneous services. The chapter further disaggregates spending by MDAs under the economic classifications of ministerial development and recurrent expenditure. Additionally, it presents the status of payables as of 31 December 2025 for the national government.
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget
heading_path: 3.2.    FY 2025/2026 Overall Budget

blocks.text: The approved gross national government budget for FY 2025/26 amounted to Kshs.4.69 trillion, representing a 7 per cent increase from Kshs.4.37 trillion in FY 2024/2025. The budget comprises Kshs.744.84 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.1.80 trillion for ministerial recurrent spending, and Kshs.2.14 trillion for CFS. Ministerial development expenditure is to be funded through the net supply (from the government exchequer) of Kshs.407.10 billion and Appropriation-in-Aid (AIA) Kshs.337.74 billion. Ministerial recurrent expenditure is to be funded by the government through the exchequer, amounting to Kshs.1,470.45 billion and AIA of Kshs.334.26 billion. In FY 2025/26, the Equitable share of revenue to County governments amounted to Kshs.415 billion. Figure 3.1 presents the budget allocation by Sector in the FY 2025/26.

blocks.text: 3.3.2  Overdraft Facility
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdraft Facility

blocks.text: The overdraft facility is a short-term borrowing facility for the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months. Kenya's Government overdraft is administered by the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). It is restricted to a maximum of five percent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdraft Facility

blocks.text: In the period under review, the overdraft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged an average interest rate of 9.41 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month. blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2025/26, compensation to employees was Kshs.337.63 billion, representing 13 per cent of the ministerial gross estimates. This did not include payments for the National Intelligence Service and the Kenya Defence Forces under the National Security Sector, and for Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies/ State Corporations/ State Owned Corporations. Considering the non-inclusions stated above, MDA 's compensation to employees accounted for 25 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally and Appropriations-in-Aid. This complies with the requirement of Regulation 26(1) 9a) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations 2015, which states that the national government's expenditure on the compensation of employees should not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of revenue raised nationally, plus other revenues generated by the national government under Article 209(4) of the Constitution. blocks.text: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR
heading_path: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR

blocks.text: 4.1.   Introduction
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. The chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first six months of FY 2025/2026. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. The chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first six months of FY 2025/2026.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: In FY 2025/2026, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.703.07 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.58.16 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector

blocks.text: 4.2.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. The ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: The State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Agriculture; and the National Land Commission (NLC), together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy, among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2025/26-2027/28, the sector plans to implement programmes that facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and the utilisation of the blue economy.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to ARUD in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.82.41 billion, compared to Kshs.81.43 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 2 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation included Kshs.48.00 billion (58
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: per cent) for development activities and Kshs.34.41 billion (42 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Agriculture received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.49.94 billion (61 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the National Land Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.36 billion (4 per cent of the ARUD Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: The high allocation to the State Department for Agriculture is due to its vital role in Agricultural Policy and Research Management, National Food Policy, Strategic Food Reserves, Crop Development, Phytosanitary Services, International Compliance, Agricultural Farmers' Training, and Agricultural Land Resource Inventory Management.

heading_path: 4.2.6   The State Department for  the Blue Economy and Fisheries

blocks.text: The State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries is mandated to coordinate the development of national oceans and blue economy strategies and policies, including Fisheries and Aquaculture Policy, as well as  the  Legal,  Regulatory,  and  Institutional  Framework  for  the  Fisheries  Industry  and  the  Blue  Economy. blocks.text: 4.3.  Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3.  Education Sector

blocks.text: 4.3.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Education Sector comprises five MDAs: the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education, the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research, the State Department for Basic Education, and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Sector envisions attaining 'Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development' in Kenya. The Sector's strategic objectives include enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development capacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: It is worth noting that the 2-6-3-3 system requires substantial infrastructure, equipment, and human capital in the medium term, from 2025/26 to 2027/28.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for the Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for the Education Sector

blocks.text: The  budgetary  allocation  to  Education  in  FY  2025/2026  amounted  to  Kshs.703.07  billion,  compared  to Kshs.681.98 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 15 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 28 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation included Kshs.29.78 billion (4 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.673.29 billion (96 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The Teachers Service Commission received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.387.18 billion (55 per cent of the Education Sector's budget), while the State Department for Science, Innovation and Research had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 0.99 billion (0.1 per cent of the Education Sector allocation).

blocks.text: The high allocation to the Teachers Service Commission is attributed to its vital role in the Teacher Resource Management programme.  Figure 4.3 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Education Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/2026.

blocks.text: 4.3.7  The Teachers Service Commission
heading_path: 4.3.7  The Teachers Service Commission

blocks.text: The Teachers Service Commission is mandated to formulate policies that regulate the teaching profession and guide teacher management functions, thereby ensuring compliance with the teaching standards prescribed from time to time. It also facilitates teachers' career progression and professional development, and monitors
heading_path: 4.3.7  The Teachers Service Commission

blocks.text: their  conduct  and  performance during curriculum implementation. TSC registers trained teachers and recruits, employs, and assigns teachers employed by the commission. It further exercises disciplinary controls over registered teachers, terminates the employment of teachers, reviews the standards of education and training for persons entering the teaching service, reviews the demand for and supply of teachers, and advises the national government on matters related to the teaching profession.

blocks.text: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector
heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector

blocks.text: 4.4.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: This Sector consists of nine MDAs: the State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs; Housing and Urban Development; Public Works; Information, Communications Technology and Digital Economy; Broadcasting and Telecommunications; Energy; and Petroleum.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The EIICT sector aims to provide sustainable infrastructure development, a vibrant shipping and maritime industry, universal access to Information and Communication Technology (ICT), Transport, and built environment services, and accessible, affordable, quality, and competitive energy and petroleum products.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The EI&ICT Sector plays a vital role as an enabler of the country's socio-economic development. It is a crucial sector in realising Vision 2030 and the BETA Agenda.

The allocation included Kshs. 380.44 billion (71 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.154.19 billion (29 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. blocks.text: 4.4.3  The State Department for Roads
heading_path: 4.4.3  The State Department for Roads

blocks.text: The State Department for Roads promotes the development of national road development policy; develops, standardises, and maintains roads; materials testing and advice on usage; protects road reserves; maintains security roads; administers mechanical and transport funds; registers engineers; provides mechanical and transport services; and enforces axle load control. The mandate is carried out by the State Department for Roads and its agencies: the Kenya Roads Board, Kenya National Highway Authority (KeNHA), Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA), Kenya Rural Roads Authority (KeRRA), Engineering Board of Kenya, and Kenya Engineering Technology Registration Board.

blocks.text: 4.4.4  The State Department for Transport
heading_path: 4.4.4  The State Department for Transport

blocks.text: The State Department for Transport promotes the management of transport policy; manage rail transport and infrastructure; fast track identified northern and LAPPSET transport corridor projects; oversight and co-ordi-
heading_path: 4.4.4  The State Department for Transport

blocks.text: nate northern corridor transport and implement Lamu South Sudan Ethiopia transit (LAPSSET) programmes; civil aviation management and training; registration and insurance of motor vehicles; motor vehicles inspection; national transport safety; national road safety management; national roads transport policy; axle load control policy and standards; develop and maintain air strips; and oversee the establish an integrated, efficient, effective and sustainable urban public transport system within the Nairobi metropolitan area. The mandate is carried out by the State Department of Transport and its agencies, the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA), Kenya Airports Authority (KAA), Kenya Railways Corporation (KRC), LAPSSET Corridor Development Authority (LCDA), Kenya Ports Authority (KPA), National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA), and the Nairobi Metropolitan Area Transport Authority (NaMATA)

blocks.text: 4.4.5  The State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs
heading_path: 4.4.5  The State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs

blocks.text: The State Department for Shipping and Maritime Affairs promotes the maritime and shipping industry; manages maritime transport; ship registration; marine cargo insurance; human resource development, management and research in support of Kenya's shipping industry; establish an effective admiralty jurisdiction; develop a central data and information centre; co-ordinate maritime spatial planning and integrated coastal zone management; protect and regulate marine ecosystems; develop national capacity for Kenya's maritime sector; promote and facilitate placement of Kenyans in the global maritime labour market; protect the aquatic resourc-
heading_path: 4.4.5  The State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs

blocks.text: es in EEZ; monitor and advising on usage of Kenya's exclusive economic zone; ocean governance and marine management; and government clearing and forwarding services. The mandate is carried out by the State Department for Shipping and Maritime Affairs and its agencies, namely the Kenya Maritime Authority (KMA), the Bandari Maritime Academy (BMA), and the Kenya National Shipping Line (KNSL).

blocks.text: 4.4.6  The State Department for Housing and Urban Development
heading_path: 4.4.6  The State Department for Housing and Urban Development

blocks.text: The State Department for Housing and Urban Development promotes the management of housing policy; manages civil servants'  housing  scheme;  develops  and  manages  affordable  housing;  national  secretariat  for human settlement; promotes low-cost house building and construction technologies; develops and manages government pool housing; shelter and slum upgrading; public office accommodation lease and management; maintain inventory of government housing property; urban planning policy; and townships, municipalities and cities policy. blocks.text: 4.4.7  The State Department for Public Works
heading_path: 4.4.7  The State Department for Public Works

blocks.text: The State Department for Public Works promotes the development of public works policy and planning; national building inspection services; sets and manages building and construction standards and codes; co-ordinate procurement of common user items by government ministries; registers and regulates contractors, consultants for buildings, civil works and material suppliers; register architects and quantity surveyors; provide mechanical and electrical building services; building research services; register and regulate civil, building and electromechanical contractors; develop and manage public buildings; building research services; and other public works. blocks.text: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector
heading_path: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: 4.5.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment and Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. The Sector also includes several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, it
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: comprises the following entities: the National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The goal of the Sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment, with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and reducing carbon emissions, improving the utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources. The Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector
heading_path: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to the EPWNR Sector in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.95.87 billion, compared to Kshs.85.37 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 2 per cent of the annual gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 4 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation comprises Kshs.61.99 billion (65 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.33.88 billion (35 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Water and Sanitation received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.53.95 billion (56 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Mining had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.63 billion (2 per cent of the Sector's allocation).

blocks.text: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector
heading_path: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector

blocks.text: 4.6.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of eight MDAs, namely the State Departments for Trade; Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development; Cooperatives; Industry; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development; Investment Promotion; East African Community; and Tourism together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The objectives of the Sector over the MTEF period are to transform Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promote and sustain tourism, promote industrial development investments, enhance trade and ease
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: of doing business, promote growth and development of cooperatives and the MSMEs Sector, promote regional integration, and promote equitable and sustainable ASAL and regional development.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector
heading_path: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to GECA in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.58.16 billion, compared to Kshs.60.90 billion allocated in FY 2024/20245. This amount represents 1 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 2 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation included Kshs.21.60 billion (37 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.36.56 billion (63 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Tourism received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.16.54 billion (28 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for the East African Community had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.03 billion (2 per cent of the GECA Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.6.3  The State Department for Trade
heading_path: 4.6.3  The State Department for Trade

blocks.text: The  State  Department  for  Trade  promotes  Trade  Policy;  Export  Development  and  Promotion;  Promote E-Commerce; Trade Negotiations and Advisory Services; Champion Trade Integration in the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), Continental Free Trade Area  (CFTA), Economic Partenership Agreement (EPA) etc.; Liaising and Coordinating with  (UNCTAD) and World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Trade Matters; Enforcement of International Trade Laws, Negotiations and Agreements; Protection of Kenyan Goods against Dumping and Subsidised Imports and recommending Countervailing Measures; Coordination
heading_path: 4.6.3  The State Department for Trade

blocks.text: of multi-Agency Task Force on the Elimination of Illicit Trade and Counterfeits; Liaison with International Trade bodies for National Development; Management of weight and measurement in Trade; Promotion and Regulation of the Wholesale and Retail Trade; and Promotion of Fair-Trade Practices and Consumer Protection. The State Department for Trade is assisted by its agencies, including the Kenya National Trading Corporation, the Kenya Export Promotion and Branding Agency, the Warehouse Receipt System Council, the Kenya Trade Remedies Agency, the Kenya Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, and the Kenya National Multi Commodities Exchange Limited.

heading_path: 4.6.4  The State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development

blocks.text: The State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development promotes Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Policy; Coordination of Planning, and Development for Arid and Semi-Arid Lands; Implementation of Special Programmes for the Development of Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Implementation of Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Programmes; Coordinating Research for sustainable Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Resource Management, De-
heading_path: 4.6.4  The State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development

blocks.text: velopment and Livelihoods; Promotion of Livestock Development, Marketing and Value addition of Resources within Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Enhancing Livelihood Resilience of Pastoral and Agro Pastoral Communities; Coordinating Responses Against Drought and Desertification; Special Programmes; Food Relief Management and Humanitarian Emergency Response; Peace Building and Conflict Management within Arid and Semi-Arid Area; Management and Promotion of Integrated Cross-border Activities in Identified ASAL Counties;  Regional  Development Policy Implementation, Oversight and Management; Coordination of Regional Development Authorities; and Projects in Response to Displacement Impacts. The mandate is carried out in collaboration with its agencies, which include the National Drought Management Authority, the Coast Development Authority, the Lake Basin Development Authority, the Ewaso Ngiro North Development Authority, the Ewaso Ngiro South Development Authority, the Tana River Development Authority, and the Kerio Valley Development Authority.

heading_path: 4.6.5  The State Department for Industry

blocks.text: The State Department for Industry promotes and facilitates domestic and Foreign Investments; Investment policy and attraction; Industrial Policy and Planning; Buy Kenya - Build Kenya Policy and Strategy; promotes
heading_path: 4.6.5  The State Department for Industry

blocks.text: standardisation in Industry and Quality Control; Kenya Property Rights Policy (Patents, Trade Marks, Service Marks, and Innovation); Promotion of Value Addition and Agro Processing; Promotion, Development and Oversight of Aggregation and Industrial Parks; Textile Sector Development; Leather Sector Development and Promotion of Value Chain; Oversight and Regulation of the Scrap Metal Industry; Industrial Training and Capacity Development; To Combat Counterfeiting, Trade and Other Dealings in Counterfeit Goods; and Oversight, Administration and Enforcement of the Local Content Policy. blocks.text: 4.6.6   The State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development
heading_path: 4.6.6   The State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development

blocks.text: The State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises(MSMEs) Development Promotes MSMEs Policy; Develop SME Financing Policy to facilitate adequate flow of credit from financial institutions; Administration of the 'Hustler Fund' for the promotion, development and enhancing competitiveness of MSMES; Capacity Development for Entrepreneurship including access to modern management practices; Support for technology upgradation and modernisation; Establishment of integrated infrastructural facilities; Promotion and  Development of  Micro  and  Small  Enterprise  and  enhance  their  competitiveness;  Promote  Progressive
heading_path: 4.6.6   The State Department for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development

blocks.text: credit policies and practices targeting MSMEs; Business Innovation and Incubation; Administer Preference in Government procurements to products and services of the MSMEs; Champion subcontracting arrangements between SMEs and Large Enterprises; Market development for MSME products and services (better access to domestic and export markets); Support for product development, design intervention and packaging; Promotion of establishment of Production clusters; and Promotion and Development of the Cottage Industry. The mandate is carried out in collaboration with its agencies, including the Uwezo Fund, the Micro and Small Enterprises Authority (MSEA), and the Kenya Industrial Estate (KIE).

blocks.text: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector

blocks.text: 4.7.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of seventeen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency (WPA); the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNHCR); the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA) and the State Department for Justice, Human Rights and Constitutional Affairs, as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Sector creates a conducive environment for the country's economic, social, and political development, which is necessary for fulfilling the objectives of Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption. It is focused on strengthening the rule of law, democracy, and human rights through various functions such as public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, and the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: This Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to GJLO in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.283.04 billion, compared to Kshs.259.82 billion allocated in the financial year 2024/2025. This amount represents 6 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 11 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation included Kshs.18.92 billion (7 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.264.12 billion (93 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for National Police Service received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.127.09 billion (45 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.530.33 million (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: The high allocation to the State Department for the National Police Service was due to the provision of security to the government's critical infrastructure and other related activities. This amount comprised Kshs.4.32 billion for development expenditure, representing 49 per cent of development net estimates, and Kshs.133.29 billion for recurrent activities, representing 51 per cent of recurrent net estimates.

The State Department for Internal Security and National Administration recorded the highest proportion of recurrent exchequer issues to recurrent net estimates of 70 per cent. blocks.text: 4.7.7  The State Law Office
heading_path: 4.7.7  The State Law Office

blocks.text: The State Law Office promotes adherence to the law by Ministries, Departments, and Agencies and is also tasked with representing the national government in legal proceedings before national, regional, and international courts and tribunals to which the national government is a party, except in criminal proceedings. blocks.text: 4.7.10  The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions
heading_path: 4.7.10  The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions

blocks.text: The Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions institutes and undertakes criminal proceedings against any person before any court of law other than the court martial and is also tasked with prosecution in respect to any offence alleged to have been committed by any person, take over and continue with any criminal proceedings commenced in any court by any person or authority with the permission of the person or authority. blocks.text: 4.8.  Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.  Health Sector

blocks.text: 4.8.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Health is primarily a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. The health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. The sector comprises two MDAs: The State Department for Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. The Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation, ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles, with a multi-sectoral approach, as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). The Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to the Health Sector in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.138.11 billion, compared to Kshs.135.19 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. This amount represents 3 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 5 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation includes Kshs.27.50 billion (20 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.110.61 billion (80 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Medical Services received the highest budget allocation of Kshs.105.95 billion (77 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards was allocated Kshs.32.15 billion (23 per cent of the Health Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for the Health Sector

blocks.text: The high allocation to the State Department for Medical Services was due to a large budget for the National Referral Services sub-programme. Figure 4.13 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Health Sector from FY 2021/2022 to FY 2025/2026.

blocks.text: 4.9.   National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.   National Security Sector

blocks.text: 4.9.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The National Security sector comprises the Ministry of Defence and the National Intelligence Service (NIS). The sector's mandate is to ensure the country's security against any threats emanating from within or outside the Kenyan borders, defend the country, and support the civil powers in maintaining peace and order.
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for the National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for the National Security Sector

blocks.text: The budget for the National Security sector in FY 2025/2026 is Kshs.253.77 billion, compared to Kshs.238.36 billion allocated in FY 2024/2025. The allocation comprised Kshs.4.93 billion for development expenditure (2 per cent of the sector's budget) and Kshs.248.84 billion for recurrent expenditure (98 per cent of the sector's allocation). The Ministry of Defence gross estimates amount to Kshs.202.32 billion (78 per cent of the sector's allocation), while NIS amounts Kshs.51.45 billion (22 per cent of the sector's allocation). The growth in the budget allocation for the National Security sector is attributed to increased funding requirements for military modernisation, enhanced territorial defence capabilities, and strengthened intelligence-gathering operations.

blocks.text: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector
heading_path: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector

blocks.text: 4.10.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely The Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State Department for National Government Coordination, State Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State Department for Special Programmes; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; The National Treasury; State Department for Public Investments and Assets Management; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; The Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; The Auditor General; The Controller of Budget, and The Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Sector provides national leadership, oversight, and policy direction towards realising the country's development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The sector has prioritised  programmes and projects aligned with the Post-COVID-19 Economic Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

The allocation included Kshs.126.83 billion (39 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.194.68 billion (61 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The National Treasury received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.106.88 billion (33 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Cabinet Affairs had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.0.23 billion (less than 1 per cent of the PAIR Sector's allocation). blocks.text: 4.11.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector
heading_path: 4.11.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector

blocks.text: 4.11.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises seven MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, Sports, Children Welfare Services, Culture, The Arts and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: The strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: The budget allocation to SPCR in FY 2025/2026 amounted to Kshs.78.99 billion, compared to Kshs.83.93 billion allocated in the previous financial year, 2024/2025. This amount represents 2 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.69 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.55 trillion. The allocation comprises Kshs.24.85 billion (31 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.54.15 billion (69 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. The State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.29.32 billion (37 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.59 billion (5 per cent of the SPCR Sector allocation).

heading_path: 4.11.5  The State Department for Children Services

blocks.text: The State Department for Children's Services promotes and safeguards the rights and welfare of all children in Kenya. blocks.text: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: In the first six months of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget identified issues that hampered budget implementation and made recommendations to address them. These issues included Low absorption of the development budget, as discussed below.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget
heading_path: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: Observation: In  the  first  six  months  of  FY  2025/26,  the  national  government's  total  expenditure  was Kshs.2,183.86 billion, representing 47 per cent of the annual gross budget. This comprised ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.276.92 billion (absorption rate of 37 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure of Kshs.899.74 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services, Kshs.1,007.20 billion (absorption rate of 47 per cent).
heading_path: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: The government directed the mandatory use of the Electronic Government Procurement System (E-GPs) by all public procuring entities, effective July 1 st, 2025, for the procurement of goods and services.   The e-GPS has posed challenges to the procurement process due to a steep learning curve for both MDAs staff and suppliers, integration issues with internal systems, and technical support problems that impact efficiency, competitiveness, and timely service delivery.   Overall, the challenges resulted in a delayed procurement process and, consequently, low absorption of the development budget.
heading_path: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: Recommendation: The Controller of Budget recommends a collaborative effort by all stakeholders in implementing the E-GPs system. This includes integration with IFMIS, training staff and suppliers in its use and technical support by timely troubleshooting issues reported.
heading_path: 5.1.  Low Absorption of Development Budget

blocks.text: 5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process
heading_path: 5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process

blocks.text: Observations: The National Treasury, in liaison with the Central Bank of Kenya and the Office of the Controller of Budget, successfully rolled out exchequer automation for the National Government except for the Public Debt, the Judiciary, County governments, second-level from County Revenue Fund to County Operational Account, Equalization Fund and some specific votes for recurrent. The Controller of Budget acknowledges the progress made in the automation process and the ongoing processes to board all the government entities.
heading_path: 5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process

blocks.text: Recommendations: To enhance efficiency and effectiveness in the approval of withdrawals from public funds, the Controller of Budget recommends automating all votes to foster efficiency and effectiveness in budget implementation. This will also add to gains on the implementation of the Treasury Single Account.
heading_path: 5.2.  Automation of Exchequer Process

blocks.text: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya provides for Supplementary appropriation for the national government to spend money that has not been appropriated if the amount appropriated for any purpose under the Appropriation Act is insufficient or a need has arisen for expenditure for a purpose for which no amount has been appropriated by that Act, or money has been withdrawn from the Contingencies Fund. The approval of Parliament for any spending under this Article shall be sought within two months after the first withdrawal of the money, subject to clause (3). Clause 5 specifies that in any particular financial year, the national government may not spend under this Article more than ten per cent of the sum appropriated by Parliament for that finan-
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: cial year unless, in exceptional circumstances, Parliament has approved a higher percentage.
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: In the first Half of FY 2025/26, the Controller of Budget has recorded an upsurge in requests for approval to release exchequer under Article 223 of the Constitution. A total of Kshs.115.11 billion was approved, comprising Public debt repayments (Kshs.86.29 billion), ministerial recurrent expenditure (Kshs.20.16 billion) and development expenditure (Kshs.8.66 billion).
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Comparatively, the withdrawals under Article 223 of the Constitution in just the first half of FY 2025/2026 surpassed full year utilization of this Article in the past three financial years. In FY 2024/25, the Cabinet Secretary of the National Treasury granted approvals of funding requests amounting to Kshs.83.96 billion, out of which the total of Kshs.66.54 billion (2 per cent) was withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund. Similarly, in FY 2023/2024 approvals by the Cabinet Secretary amounted to Kshs.30.66 billion out of which Kshs.19.12 billion (less than 1 per cent) was withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund. Further, cumulative withdrawals under Article 223 for FY 2022/2023 totalled Kshs.69.20 billion (2 per cent).
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: In many instances, these withdrawals under Article 223 were for regular operations and the settlement of pending bills, which clearly demonstrate the existing weaknesses in the budgeting cycle. Increased use of Article 223 is likely to circumvent the budget process and credibility.
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: Recommendation: The Controller of Budget recommends adopting sound planning, budget practices, and effective expenditure management by prioritising essential services and aligning them with operational realities during budget formulation and implementation. In addition, the Cabinet Secretary for National Treasury should expedite the submission of necessary documentation to Parliament for approval within the stipulated two-month period to ensure compliance with constitutional requirements. In addition, the Controller of Budget recommends a review of the legislative framework governing the criteria for funding under Article 223 of the Constitution, as well as the mechanisms for controls to ensure fiscal integrity and safeguard budget transparency.
heading_path: 5.3.  Exchequer Issues under Supplementary - Use of Article 223 of the Constitution

blocks.text: 6. EMERGING ISSUES
heading_path: 6. EMERGING ISSUES

blocks.text: 6.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 6.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: This chapter presents emerging issues that the Controller of Budget has identified and calls for attention by the government.
heading_path: 6.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025
heading_path: 6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025

blocks.text: Total public and publicly guaranteed debt has been on the rise over the years. The increase is driven by annual borrowing by the national government to finance the budget deficit and also to obtain additional funds to pay accumulated interest on the debt stock carried over from previous years. The public debt stock increased from Kshs.11,799.66 billion (67.8 percent of GDP) in June 2025 to Kshs.12,287.58 billion in December 2025. The fiscal deficit at the beginning of the FY 2024/25 was Kshs 1,010 billion (5.8 percent of GDP) and is expected to reduce to Kshs. 876.10 billion (4.5 percent of GDP) according to the 2026 Budget Policy Statement (BPS).
heading_path: 6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025

blocks.text: As at December 2025, domestic debt stock was Kshs.6,825.61 billion, an increase from Kshs.6,311.20 billion, as of 30 th June 2025, while the external debt stock decreased to Kshs. 5,461.97 billion, from Kshs. 5,488.46 billion in June 2025. Borrowing from the domestic market is undertaken primarily through Treasury Bills and Bonds, comprising 97.5 percent of the total domestic debt, an indicator that other elements of domestic debt, such as the Central Bank overdraft to the national government, constitute only a small proportion of the domestic debt. While domestic borrowing contributes positively to the development of the domestic debt market, increased borrowing leads to high domestic interest rates, which in turn lead to reduced investment due to the high cost of borrowing, crowding out private sector investments. Table 6.1 shows the composition of domestic debt as 31 st  December 2025.

blocks.text: As shown in Table 6.1, the amount of overdraft from the Central Bank to the National Government increased by Kshs.10.6 billion over the last six months to Kshs.78.23 billion. Given that the Central Bank lending rate decreased from 9.75 percent in June 2025 to 9.0 percent in December 2025, the increase in the overdraft can be attributed to additional borrowing from the Central Bank of Kenya. Over the review period, the Pre-1997 Government overdraft decreased marginally by Kshs. 0.55 billion as at 31st December 2025. Currently, the government pays 3 percent interest on the outstanding balance of the Pre-1997 Government debt. Further, the amount owed to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) was reduced by Kshs. 5.18 billion as a result of the government's increased payments.
heading_path: 6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025

blocks.text: An analysis of domestic debt based on holders of domestic debt shows that financial institutions, such as Commercial Banks and Insurance Companies, held the highest amount of domestic debt, amounting to Kshs.5,247 billion as at 31 st December 2025, representing an increase of Kshs.149.67 billion lent to the government over
heading_path: 6.1.1  Status of Domestic Debt Stock, as at 31 st  December 2025

blocks.text: the first half of the FY 2025/26. The high holdings of domestic debt by Financial Corporations can be attributed to the high interest rates charged on the government treasury bills and bonds, attracting high returns with no associated risk. It also points to the increasing crowding of the private sector borrowers from the domestic debt market, as commercial banks prefer investing in treasury Bills and bonds with guaranteed returns. The high interest rates in the domestic market has also attracted the interest of non-residents, who increased their holdings of domestic debt by Kshs. 8.46 billion to Kshs.311.27 billion as at 31 st December 2025. Non-profit institutions held the least amount of domestic debt over the period July 2025 to 31 st December 2025 at Kshs.56.47 billion. blocks.text: 6.2.  Domestic Debt Budget Performance
heading_path: 6.2.  Domestic Debt Budget Performance

blocks.text: In the first half of FY 2025/26, the total domestic debt payment was Kshs.545.90 billion, consisting of Kshs.183.66 billion and Kshs.362.24 billion for principal and interest payments, respectively. The total revenue collected during the same period was Kshs.1,243.40 billion, indicating 44 percent of the revenue was used to service domestic debt. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) recommends a threshold for total debt service (both domestic and external debt service) to revenue of 30 per cent, indicating that Kenya's debt service costs on domestically borrowed funds alone exceed the IMF-recommended threshold for overall debt by 14.13 percent. The high debt service costs can be attributed to high interest payments on Treasury bills and bonds. High debt service leads to a reduction in total revenues as funds collected from taxes are used to service the debt. When a high proportion of the collected revenues are used to service debt, it limits the ability of the government to implement other programmes and offer services to the public. This situation underscores the challenges faced by the government in managing its debt obligations while striving to maintain fiscal sustainability.
heading_path: 6.2.  Domestic Debt Budget Performance

blocks.text: 6.3.  Recommendations
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: To effectively manage the high domestic borrowing and the associated high interest rates, the government may consider the following:
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: Put in measures to reduce the fiscal deficit in the medium term in line with the projections of the 2025 Budget Policy Statement.
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: Aim to implement the provisions of the 2025 Medium-Term Debt Strategy that recommends a borrowing mix of 50:50 for domestic to external borrowing. This will reduce the over-reliance on domestic borrowing.
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: The government's 2025 Medium-Term Debt Strategy (MTDS) aimed to reduce reliance on short-term debt instruments like Treasury Bills and lengthen the maturity profile of public debt. This strategy is designed to mitigate refinancing risks and ensure debt sustainability.
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: The government may implement appropriate monetary policies to ensure a reduction in the domestic interest rates. The government should ensure that the adopted policies provide a conducive environment for the private sector to operate.
heading_path: 6.3.  Recommendations

blocks.text: 7. CONCLUSION
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: The National Government Budget Implementation Review Report is prepared in fulfillment of Article 228(6) of the Constitution, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit a report on the implementation of budgets for national and county governments to each House of Parliament every four months. It provides an overview of financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first six months of FY 2025/26 in line with Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which outlines the information to be published in the report. These included actual receipts into the Consolidated Fund, approved budget, funds released, total expenditure and project implementation.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.2.17 trillion, representing 49 per cent of the annual target. The Controller of Budget approved withdrawals of Kshs.2.15 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 48 per cent of the net annual estimates. Ministries, Departments and Agencies received Kshs.954.23 billion, representing 51 per cent of the net annual estimates, comprising Kshs.145.03 billion for ministerial development expenditure (36 per cent of the net annual estimates) and Kshs.809.19 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure (55 per cent of the net annual estimates). Consolidated Fund Services received Kshs.1.02 trillion, and County Governments received Kshs.172.23 billion as an equitable share of revenues raised nationally, representing 48 per cent and 42 per cent of the annual net estimates, respectively.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: The Gross accrued expenditure for the National Government in the period under review was Kshs.2.18 trillion, representing an absorption rate of 47 per cent, comprising ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.276.92 billion (absorption rate of 37 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure of Kshs.899.74 billion (absorption rate of 50 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.1.01 trillion (absorption rate of 47 per cent). The absorption was within the prorated target of 50 per cent in the first six months, except the ministerial development budget, which was at 37 per cent.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: While overseeing budget implementation in the first six months of the financial year, the Controller of Budget identified Key issues and recommended how they should be addressed to enhance effective budget implementation. These included: low absorption of development budget, Automation of the exchequer process and Use of Supplementary Budget under Article 223 of the Constitution to fund government programmes.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: The Controller of Budget appreciates the government directive to roll out the Electronic Procurement System aimed at enhancing transparency, equity, and cost-effectiveness in the use of public resources. The teething challenges facing the process have been identified, and we recommend a timely address to hasten the procurement process and subsequent implementation of the development programmes.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: The Controller of Budget recommends that the national government, through the National Treasury, fast-track automation of the exchequer process for all Votes, the Public Debt, the Equalization Fund and level two transfer of funds from the County Revenue Fund to County Operations Accounts for the County governments. This will reduce turnaround time and ensure timely approval of withdrawals from public funds and the timely delivery of services.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: On the issues of Supplementary Estimates under Article 223 of the Constitution, the Controller of Budget recommends a review of the legislative framework to provide for clear criteria for funding under Article 223 and the mechanisms for controls to ensure fiscal integrity and safeguard budget transparency.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Finally, regarding the increase in domestic debt, the Controller of Budget recommends government intervention to avert adverse effects emanating from over-reliance on domestic borrowing to meet the budget deficit.
heading_path: 7. CONCLUSION
